utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, yesterday when we left off, just to assist you in catching up, we discussed the issue of Mr. Vujica and his affiliation in special units. You indicated that he was wearing a Jokers patch and, in fact, there was no attempt to hide that. Continuing from that point, did you spend any time at all with Mr. Vujica for any reason while you were at Kratine?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I spent the whole night with him, because when we reached the Kratine, we were asked to dig trenches, and we did until nightfall. However, as I wear contact lenses, I can't see very well at night. So I asked him to release me of this duty during the night, so that I shouldn't hurt myself or something like that. And then he said that was okay, and that I could stay with him. So we spent the whole night together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Vujica from any previous time, or did any member of your family know Mr. Vujica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Actually, when we got there, he recognised me. I didn't recognise him immediately, because he knew my wife, who is from Busovaca. And so they knew each other. I don't know exactly whether they went to school together or worked together. And since I would go there often, he recognised me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the course of your discussions with him during the night, did you discuss any aspect of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: In the course of our conversations, which focused on some very general questions, I mentioned that I didn't know what had happened to our house down there. And his answer, when I -- when he asked me to explain where the house was situated, I did so, and he said that the house was most certainly destroyed, that I shouldn't count on it, because it no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, this discussion took place approximately one week after the incident at Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, roughly so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have any conclusions or fears -- excuse me -- any conclusions about the level of Mr. Vujica's knowledge after that conversation, knowledge relative to the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, judging by the way he told me what had happened to our house, my conclusion was that either he had been there at the time or immediately afterwards. I do believe that he had relevant data about the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Returning to the discussion about Miroslav Bralo, whom you also heard called Cicko. Did Bralo force any of the persons in your company or yourself to do anything which contravened your own religious practices?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. When we got there, when we had been brought to Kratine, Cicko said something like, "You can't begin working until you cross yourself. Those are our customs." And he asked who of us knew how to make the sign of the cross. I happened to know. And he told me that I should teach all the others, because those who didn't know would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, were the others also all Muslims, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Absolutely all of them. At least the group of five or six of us who came there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Bralo have any weapons that suggested that he might, in fact, carry out his threat to kill?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: At the time, that is while we were there, he didn't have any weapon on him, except an axe, and he threatened with this axe. And he threatened to kill us with an axe. He would wave this axe about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions under which you were forced to dig trenches at Kratine, including the number of days and whether or not you were provided with rest?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The group I was in stayed for about four nights, as far as I can remember. We worked during the night and the day, with occasional rests for about half an hour, and then during the night perhaps for two or three hours we were allowed to rest. The conditions under which we worked were such that we were on the front line. There was crossfire, so that we were in a situation in which we were exposed to danger. But luckily no one in the group was hurt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One last quick question on this point. Where was the Kuber feature relative to the front line?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The Kuber feature was slightly above; that is, at least they said it was Kuber. And between us and Kuber, there was a valley of some 300 metres, and Kuber was just above. That is the positions from where the fire came at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On or about the 25th of April, did you observe any violence by Bralo upon detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We were in a trench which was just behind the house in which HVO soldiers rested, and I think it was one afternoon when I saw Cicko with three young men, and he ordered them to run around a stable, to lie down, to get up, to crawl and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know their fate?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but this HVO soldier who was in the trench where we were, he said, "The fool is bound to kill them."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on to your time after release from Kratine, which occurred approximately the 26th -- I'm sorry, when you were visited by the Red Cross at Kratine, which was about the 26th of April, when did you actually leave Kratine and where were you returned to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: This might have been -- though I'm not sure of any dates, but it was some four or five days after we had been taken there. We were brought back late at night, about midnight, to the SDK building from where we had been taken in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And then from there, did you go anywhere for final registration before being released?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. We were in the SDK building for a couple of days, and then the guards who were guarding us said we could go home, as if we had been released. But before that, we had to go to the cinema building, where we were registered for the Red Cross, and on the way out, we were also registered by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know who registered you, and what was the type of questioning that was addressed in that registration? What were you asked about?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I know. A young woman was there. I knew her by sight from town. Her name was Badrov, her surname, rather. I know because she had a brother who played basketball, so I knew the family. She was wearing a camouflage uniform. And apart from the essential data like name, date and so on, the question was whether we wanted to stay in Vitez or to leave in the direction of Travnik or Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was Ms. Badrov wearing any HVO patches, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. HVO, I think she had on her sleeve, or a badge on her pocket. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you were to go to either Zenica or Travnik, how did the HVO propose to get you there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: As we were leaving the cinema building, buses were already parked in front, and those who were ready to go could leave immediately. This option was available on a daily basis. If I recollect well, I think there were a couple of buses leaving in both directions around 11 every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And those buses were provided by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I suppose so, because I don't see anyone else doing it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what decision did you make about staying or leaving Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: My family and I had spent some 25 or 24 years in Vitez, so we just couldn't conceive of the idea of leaving. We could never imagine having to leave Vitez. So we thought -- we were all persuaded that this wouldn't last long and that we should endure for a couple of days and that things would settle down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can speed things up. You decided to stay in Vitez, did you, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help me with this: You mentioned the SDK building. What was it used for before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: It was a building of the institute for payments, public auditing, so that various payments were made in the premises; for instance, if you took your driver's test, and also for any transfer of payments from one company to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it was an office, office building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you returned to your apartment building, do you recall any conversations you had with an HVO soldier by the name of Ivica from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. Quite by chance, I met him. He would come to visit the area occasionally, and he would enter the basements where most of us were. He would help some people by giving them some cigarettes or medicine, so obviously he was in charge of that particular district. One day, we were in my apartment, having coffee, and again we had a general discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did the discussion turn to the morning of April the 16th, and if it did, what was said by Ivica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, quite by chance. I can't remember the context of the conversation, but I do remember that he said that he was woken up at 2 in the morning, on the 16th, that there was an alarm, and that they had to go into action. And then, having realised that he had revealed more than he wanted, he said -- he added, "We were expecting an attack."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where was Ivica's unit based? Where was he housed at the time, in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: In the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on to about the 15th of May. Do you recall an incident in which a Golf vehicle with soldiers approached your apartment building? HVO soldiers, if I may add that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. Of course, I don't remember the exact date. But I remember the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were any or all of the soldiers wearing any patches which may have suggested they were in special units?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Let me see. Since they was some 20 or 30 metres away, I did not see the insignia on their uniforms. But as my wife and I were on the balcony at the time, she did see it, and she even recognised an old acquaintance of hers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I think she told me that the guy's name was Oliver Petrovic. They went to the same elementary school together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did she at that moment describe to you the type of patch which she saw?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. She said they were Jokers. And that's what she said, "The Jokers had come, and I recognised Oliver."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to please show to the witness a piece of paper bearing a name which should not be read out loud, if he identifies it, and should remain under seal after shown to the bench and counsel. Please do not comment out loud. Mr. Ahmic, with reference to the name which you have seen, do you recognise that name, again without mentioning it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Connected with the incident of the HVO soldiers, at least one of whom was wearing a Jokers patch that day, what happened with the woman whose name is on that piece of paper, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The soldiers who came in that vehicle, I think there were five of them -- four or five soldiers; two or three of them entered the building. And just then my wife and I went to the other room, because it wasn't a good idea to be seen when soldiers were around the building. So we went to the other room and we peeped out behind the curtain. And we saw them take this person out, the person whose name was on this piece of paper. They put her in the car and drove off. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know this person? Had she been a long-time resident of that building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember -- for as long as I can remember, she had been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you recall, were any of her family members with her at the time, without giving names?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were two members of the family, two children, and I think that the husband was not in Vitez at all at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on to the 8th or 9th of June. Was your apartment entered by any HVO soldiers in the early hours of the morning, and if so, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was sometime late in the evening, perhaps after 12, or around about 1 a.m., we were getting ready to go to bed. Somebody knocked on the door. I opened the door, and a soldier stormed in, carrying a pistol. He came into our apartment. And I saw two other men, because the candlelights were on in the corridor. The other stood in front of the door, and the other one was by the staircase. But just one of them went into our apartment. He pushed me into the bathroom straightaway. And he said: What are we waiting for? Why are we still there? And that he would be back the next day, and he didn't want to see us there when he came back. He hit me once in the region of my stomach. He kicked me with his leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was the weapon drawn and pointed at anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was pointed at me. When he came in, when I opened the door and he stormed in, he pushed me into the bathroom with his pistol, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Between the time you returned to your apartment, after being released from detention, and that incident, had you observed much expulsion activity of Muslims in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way. At that time certain things were heard, and rumours as well. But what happened was that people who were in the other part of town began leaving their apartments first; that is to say, not in the area we lived in, but in the other part of town. So that it was our turn somewhere towards the end. But up until then, perhaps -- well, I don't know. Maybe all the people, or very few families, actually, remained in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say they were leaving their apartment, were they leaving voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Absolutely not, because I know some people who thought the same as we did. That is to say, they wouldn't -- they didn't want to leave their homes at any price. But everything was done under force, absolutely. So a large number were directly forced to leave and, of course, some of the other people probably saw the first people leave, so they decided to leave as well. And it was the HVO soldiers which entered all the apartments later on, which is indicative.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know someone named Slaven Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is he related to Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: It's his brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you go to him for any assistance in this interim period?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At that time, the command post, Darko's command post, was in a building which was at the other part of town, and they spent a lot of time in the Benz Cafe. And I went there and found Slaven and asked him to help me, if possible. That is to say, to help me remain in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. We are of the same generation, and we went to primary school together. We went and did eight years of primary school together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he help you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, conditionally speaking, yes. But he helped me, and I use inverted commas when I say the word "help," he helped me in the following way. He said, if I really wished to stay, then we'll try and put his name and surname on the door of my apartment, and that that should have some effect on any people coming to evict us. Which is what I did, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did that have the desired effect of preventing your eviction?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, as I said a moment ago, regardless of that, we were thrown out of the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who assisted you, if anyone, in leaving Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: As we saw that night that there was nothing to be done, we made a decision and we decided to go towards Zenica, because some of our family members are there, quite a large number, and so we tried to find a way to do this. And I also asked another of my colleagues who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was that and what nationality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: His name was Miroslav Pavlovic, and he was a Croat from, well, Stari Vitez, who was in that part of town because several days prior to that, he too had taken up residence in somebody else's apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving quickly, can you tell us what, if any, possessions you took with you and how you left Vitez physically, what the means were?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, as we knew the crossing was to take place in a place called Safradini, which is the old road towards Zenica, we just took what we could carry with us, because we had to cross on foot some 400 or 500 metres. So we had two bags or plastic bags; I don't know. But I asked Miroslav to transfer us from Vitez down to the railway station and the crossroads, the junction towards Zenica, from which point we were to go on foot and cross over to the territory which was held by the BiH Army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Pavlovic take you to that point he said he would, and did he assist you further?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: He said that he would have to go down there first to see whether there was any possibility of leaving at the time because there was some shooting, and when the alarm was sounded, no crossings were possible. So he went down there and allegedly had checked out the situation. He came back very quickly, 10 to 15 minutes later, and he said that everything was okay, that he had asked and that we could start. So we put our things into the car, we packed them in his car, and he took us to the crossroads and left us down there and came back himself. We had to wait for a while for some soldiers to come up and tell us when we could cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did soldiers come and tell you, and were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The soldiers were HVO, and from time to time -- we stood there for some 40 minutes, perhaps an hour; I don't quite remember. But a soldier would come up to us from time to time to tell us we couldn't cross yet because an alarm had sounded or something like that. In about an hour's time, a man turned up; whether by chance or not, I don't know. But he knew my father, and he said that he would give us a lift in his car and take us to the Krizancevo Selo area, thereabouts, from where we would have less to walk and we would pass the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is Krizancevo Selo in Vitez, and was it a military base for any particular group?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's in Vitez, it's situated in Vitez. We were brought to a place which they called a command or something like that, although it didn't look much like a headquarters from outside. It was a house belonging to a man, and together with this -- next to this house was a sort of cafe, or a shop, or something like that, a facility like that. So that's where he took us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who is Vlado Krizanac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Vlado Krizanac was a man, that is to say, whose house that was, and as far as I was able to notice, he was a sort of Commander over there. I don't know what his function was. He belonged to the Vitezovi. That's a fact that I know for sure. The soldiers would come up to him from time to time to ask him something, and he would give out some orders, issue some orders or information, something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Vlado Krizanac have any patches that suggested he was with the Vitezovi, as you believe?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had the Vitezovi patch on his shoulder, and he didn't hide that fact, at least from the conversation I had with him. He said that at the beginning of the war, he was one of the founders of HOS in Vitez and that Darko Kraljevic would come frequently while we were there, that -- Darko Kraljevic visited him. I didn't hear their conversation, they didn't talk in the house, but that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you personally observe Darko Kraljevic visiting Vlado Krizanac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He would come there. They would sit around in that sort of cafe. It was some five metres in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krizanac use any other name?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, everybody in his family and the other people that came to him called him Sidi, as far as I was able to hear. That's what he was called, Sidi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where did you stay while you were in Krizancevo Selo, and for how long?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: In Krizancevo Selo, well, we stayed there -- that is to say, the day we thought we would cross over to the other side, they told us that we couldn't cross on that particular day. And then Sidi's wife, because she knew my mother, suggested we go into their house and have a cup of coffee and a rest. But we stayed there, in fact, for about four days or four nights. Four to five days was the time we spent in that house in a sort of -- in a house-detention capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How, ultimately, were you able to go to Zenica. Were you able to do so unconditionally?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: For the first two days, roughly -- well, the first day, that is, the day after we had arrived, the same story repeated itself. We asked whether we could cross over. They said we couldn't. They said the alarm had sounded again or something of that kind. However, later on Sidi's brother came by, and another man wearing a uniform, and they told my father that he ought to cross over to Zenica and to bring -- they gave him a piece of paper which had some names and surnames and addresses on it and, I think, some telephone numbers as well of people whom he ought to find in Zenica. And only when he had brought these people from Zenica, he said, would we be able to leave. So they would only let us go after my father had done this for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were these people in Zenica Croats, Muslims, or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: They were Croats, members of -- family members of that particular man who had come to us. His daughter, two children, and her husband. I think there were two aunts as well of this Sidi person and his brother, and the daughter and son as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just to clarify, then, your father was to go alone, you were to remain behind with your mother and wife, and if, in fact, he could bring back some or all of these people, then possibly you would be exchanged. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what was the result of your father's search?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, he found all the people that he was asked to find except one man who was, at the time, at the KP in Zenica, a member of the HVO, and he was a prisoner in the house of correction, and he wasn't able to get him out of the prison. And one -- the daughter of this other man gave -- made a statement in writing on a piece of paper that she did not wish to leave Zenica, and I think she gave a brief explanation, so that my father came back with two aunts and the daughter of one of those aunts, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then you were released, and where did you go after you were released?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, yes, on that day, it was sometime around 10.00 in the morning, my father, first of all, came with one of the aunts, and he told Sidi and the other one, "There's another aunt and her daughter up there," and that we should be released. And that's what happened. They put us in a car and took us off to near the demarcation line. We crossed over the line to the side -- the territory that was under BiH control, and we were temporarily put up in the village of Poculica, which is two or three kilometres off.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did something happen to you physically there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Would you clarify where you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you injured while you were in the Poculica area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I was injured, probably by a sniper. My right arm and chest, lungs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever come to learn what happened with your apartment in Vitez, after you were forced out?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, we learnt what had happened. A young man took up residence in our apartment, whom I knew from town previously, with his wife and, I think, two children. And he is in the flat until this very day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you making efforts to try to get your flat back? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Shortly after you were released from detention in Vitez, did you return to Ahmici, the village where your house was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you observe the condition of Croat houses in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: In that part, that is to say the road we take in order to reach our own house, there are houses on both sides, so we had to pass through that part of the village. And you could clearly see. Of course, I didn't know all the houses, and who all the houses belonged to, but the houses belonging to our family, the Muslim houses, the ones I knew about, all of them had been burnt. Whereas, as to the Croatian houses belonging to our Croat neighbours, I didn't see a single burnt down house. So this was indicative. And in that part of town, for example, two houses were burnt, and then one wasn't burnt, then one would be burnt, and three would not be burnt. So it was selectively done. The burning was selectively carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your dealings, whether in person or verbally, with Dario Kordic. Looking back to 1992, did you ever personally come in contact with Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I couldn't say that I had any personal contact with him. I didn't know him, personally. I knew who he was, of course, and things like that. But we were very close by, on one occasion, so that I was able to see him, because we were standing close by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you, very briefly, describe the circumstances of that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, it was on the day the attack was launched by the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army on Busovaca. And at the time we were sitting around on the terrace of a cafe, and we saw the shelling down there. And we were just thinking where it would be best to take shelter, because it was a terrible thing to have happened for us. We'd never encountered anything like that. So we rushed to premises below the post office, which was the information and alert centre. That was what it was called. And we knew there was a basement there that was safe and was secure against shelling. We thought we would get information as to what was going on. We were interested in what was going on. So myself and some of my friends went down there, as we knew some of the young men, some of the guys that worked there. And I think that it was in one -- one or two hours later that Mr. Kordic turned up with -- escorted by two or three soldiers, I think, and he entered this premises. So that was the occasion on which I met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This was, if bombings were involved, in 1992, and you were in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How was Mr. Kordic dressed, when you saw him at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform, had a cap on his head. He didn't have any long-barrelled weapons. I didn't see if he had a pistol or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was he alone or was he escorted?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: He was escorted. He was escorted by two or three soldiers who came in with him, also wearing uniforms. And he went into the information centre, as it was called, and I think that the guys with him said -- that is to say, I saw a person in uniform, and I think they said his name was Filip Filipovic. I didn't know him, to be frank, but I did see him later on on the local television. And Mr. Kordic went into an office with this person and they talked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the issue of television, did you ever see Mr. Kordic and any of the either members of the BiH or TO in any discussions, particularly at the end of 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kordic was a guest on television very frequently, so that we were able to see him almost daily; if not live, then they would be repetitions of some programmes he had taken part in. And one particular programme would be, perhaps, interesting, and that was one I myself took part in. There was a call-in type of programme, an open programme inviting questions from viewers, and I myself asked a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the question you asked, and why did you ask it? And of whom did you ask it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kordic was a guest on the programme, together with Sefkija Djidic, I think it was, and they were speaking on current affairs, relations between the Army and BiH and the Croatian Defence Council and things like that. And I didn't like a statement made by Mr. Kordic, in which he said that the Croats should solve their own national question, both territorially and nationally. And this was -- I didn't think he finished off what he was -- what he meant to say. So I phoned the telephone number up and asked Mr. Kordic directly: What, in that case, would happen to the Muslims? What should be done with the Muslims, if he was to go ahead with what he said? And this was read out on television, along with my name and surname. They said who had asked the question. However, I did not receive an answer, because it was -- they were very -- they politically side-stepped the issue, if I could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, we would like to reverse the order of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness, my name is Bozidar Kovacic, and together with my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez. I have a few questions for you, so I appeal to you for patience. Also, we speak the same language, and you know that we have simultaneous interpretation, so we must speak slowly and make a pause between the questions and answers. Tell me, please, at the beginning you told us about your career and how you joined the Territorial Defence. If I understood you correctly, you were mobilised to work in the Territorial Defence in June, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, please be kind enough and tell me, when you were mobilised, there were virtually no Croats left in the Territorial Defence, were there? Could you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: There were, as far as I can remember, maybe two guys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can it be said, then, that, in fact, at the time there was a kind of ethnic grouping along ethnic lines, generally speaking at least, within Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: From the military standpoint, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there was already a separation between the two groups that was quite visible?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, on the day the conflict started, on the 16th of April, 1993, you said that you heard the sounds of explosions in Stari Vitez. In view of the position of your building, you couldn't really see it; it was just your conclusion on the basis of what you heard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: May I give a brief explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The building I lived in is about 150 to 200 metres away from the line of attack against Stari Vitez, so if shells are falling at a distance of 150 to 200 metres, you can hear them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Quite. Does that mean that your building is in the first row of buildings behind the hotel, in the opposite direction from Stari Vitez; Stari Vitez, the hotel, and then your buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. It is the row in front. My building is the second building next to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. So after the 16th of April, your building was virtually on the front line, or on the line of separation forces, in Stari Vitez and in Vitez itself?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Not quite. About 100 metres away was the line, because the road behind the market, and the garages in Stari Vitez were actually on the line of separation. So my building is about 150 metres away from that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the camouflaged soldiers, whom you called Vitezovi. You mentioned a person called Robert Safradin, whom you had known from before. But let me ask you this: This surname, Safradin, is a frequent surname in that part of Central Bosnia; is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I know there is a part, an area called Safradin, so in Vitez, perhaps, but for -- as for Busovaca, Novi Travnik, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, in any case, there are quite a number of people called Safradin in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: One could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The other two who, with Safradin, who went to your apartment and removed their mask, you didn't recognise them as locals?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Let me make -- let me give you an explanation, if I may. I didn't recognise them as people I had seen in town. Since I have been in Vitez for 25 years, I knew everyone. It's a small town, as you probably know. I knew everyone living there in town and in the immediate surroundings. So these men were not from the town proper. They may have been from Vitez municipality, but I didn't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Or they may have come from outside the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: They may have come from outside Vitez, but they were certainly from Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You told us that on the 19th of April, members of the Military Police appeared in front of your apartment, and explained to you that for security reasons there may be angry soldiers in town, so that, for the sake of your security, they were taking you to the SDK building. Did you accept their story as a truthful one, or did you consider this to be a mere excuse to take you away?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I think it was just an excuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. After spending a couple of days in the SDK, and after leaving, is it right to say that it was chaotic in town, that there were people who were quite furious, and that some people were killed for no proper reason?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: There were incidents, but I wouldn't agree that they -- the cause were individuals who were quite out of control. At least not in all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So will you come to the point when you were in the SDK, as you told us. Did anything happen to any of the detainees in the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that in this place of detention in the SDK building, that the guards in that building treated the detainees quite correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: In view of the prevailing conditions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There was no mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, not in the classical sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You had enough to eat and drink?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Family visits were allowed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Family members could bring you some essentials?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that several people were taken to see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember that particular detail, but probably -- you're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As for hygiene, as far as facilities allowed, could you use the toilet, water and everything?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that occasionally this person nicknamed Zabac, Kovac, would come in a vehicle clearly marked as belonging to the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Markings of the Military Police? I do not remember that there were any clear signs of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were Military Police insignia clear on him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. He wore the typical white belt worn by the Military Police, and he carried a pistol, and on his sleeve he had a patch saying "Military Police."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You told us that personally -- sorry, let me scratch that. You saw Cerkez on television, you said, and at the time you knew that he was an Officer in the HVO. Later on, you realised that Cerkez was obviously some sort of a Commander or, rather, a Brigade Commander. I think that is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion personally to see Cerkez as an HVO Officer formally communicating with other HVO members or any other event when he would act in his capacity of an HVO Commander?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: With the exception of his appearances on television, I did not have occasion to see personally him issuing any orders. But as my building is in the immediate vicinity of the hotel, I saw him a couple of times coming out with an escort, getting into military vehicles, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about '92, the beginning of '93?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, roughly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know exactly the name of the Unit of which Cerkez was the Commander at the time when the conflict broke out on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was called the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Quite correct, thank you. And do you know whether that Brigade had its Command Headquarters in the building of the Workers' University, popularly known as the cinema building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I think that they were in the hotel. How they were organisationally structured, I don't know. As far as my friends said, the headquarters was in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with that. Does the name "Colonel Blaskic" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. It was a similar situation as with Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Without going into any detail, we know from your previous statement that you knew that Blaskic held a superior position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, just a moment. What is the point of this cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What is the point of the cross-examination? We know the position, as far as authority was concerned, in the HVO. This witness can, with respect to him, add absolutely nothing on this particular topic. Now, we are, I suspect, wasting time by going over the same points over and over again. Unless there's something knew which this witness can say, and you can point it out, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is nothing knew, Your Honour. It was just I was trying to establish what, really, the witness knows about the hierarchy and organisation of the HVO, since he mentioned a not really very defined relationship between Cerkez and Darko Kraljevic. And that is my only purpose, and if I may now conclude with that question and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask him about that relationship, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, from what you told us about a possible relationship between Darko Kraljevic's unit and Cerkez, can you assert, on the basis of anything, that Cerkez was the superior to Darko Kraljevic's unit?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: My statement about this matter is based on the following, and that is that the HVO was much, much better organised than the BH Army, and what we were able to conclude about the concept of the HDZ authority and the HVO was that they were highly organised, so there was nothing loose in their relationship. If he was the Commander of the Vitez Brigade, he was the Commander of the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is your assessment?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I am sure you will realise I cannot have any document to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But that is just your conclusion on the basis of what you saw? You never saw any document, any assertion of somebody who knew about that for sure from the inside?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Of course, I didn't see any document, and these things were not being concealed at all at the time in Vitez, who was a member of which Unit, who commanded whom. This was nothing that was secret at the time in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You gave a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal earlier on. This was a year ago yesterday. On page 2, you said, in the first paragraph, that: "Everyone knew who was the Commander of the Vitezovi. I didn't have knowledge about the chain of command above Darko." Do you agree that that is what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: It's probably what I said. It was a year ago. I can't remember it. If you have a more concrete question, I shall answer it gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. All you know about it is your own judgement, your own assessment, on the basis of general views?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A detailed point in connection with the trench-digging that was not touched upon in your direct examination. You said that you were first taken to the positions at Vranjska and that you stayed there until about 2.00 or 3.00 that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then the Military Police took you again to this other location at Kratine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your earlier statement, you said that from Vranjska you were first taken to the Bungalow, and from there, with another means of transport, to Kratine. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. The Bungalow is on the way to Kratine, so we just stopped there and the members of the escort entered the Bungalow. I don't know what they were doing there. They told us we could get off the bus and light a cigarette, if anyone wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this first location where you were digging at Vranjska, that is a part of Rijeka, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, the area where we were is a part of Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you said that there were no incidents there and no mistreatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you worked at a normal rate, you had breaks, you could have a smoke, you got food and drinks?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't think we were given any food there, because we didn't spend much time there, but that was not the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you were there for a couple of hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you able to identify the unit holding that position at Vranjska, at Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I think it was, as there were local there, local guys, some of them -- I knew some of them, so they were probably local people from Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us agree regarding the position of Kratine. Do you know the rough borders of Vitez municipality? Do you know that Kratine is on the actual border towards Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the part of Kratine where you were digging is only some half a kilometre west of the place called Loncari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I've never been to Loncari, so judging by what the guy showed us, it could be there somewhere, roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness Ahmic, you were taken to that position at Kratine by the Military Police. Was that just one position or several linked positions along the edge of that plateau that you referred to? As far as you could see, of course.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't know, in military terms, whether they were separated or not. All I can testify about is the area where I was. It looked like a unified hold to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you able to notice whether there was several military units, a single military unit?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: To me personally, this was rather interesting, because I too was a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: So what I found interesting was that the front-line soldiers were the Jokers. The gentleman I referred to earlier on, Ivica Vujica, was a member of the Jokers, and they called him the Commander of the Front Line. He would drive us from one trench to another and tell us where to dig trenches. He was there, I think, for two days. Later on, another gentleman came who was again a member of the Jokers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you deduced from that that this area was under the Jokers' control?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Absolutely so -- absolutely no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But who then controlled it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The regular units of the HVO. And only for those four days, the Jokers held those lines for some reason. Those lines were under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And those that you referred to as regular HVO units, were they from Vitez or from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I think they were mostly local people, but there were quite a number of guys from Zenica and Busovaca. I learned this from their conversation, but they were all from Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a conversation with an HVO member in the hotel who somehow let himself go and said things he didn't intend to say. From that conversation, was it clear that this Ivica was also a member of the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. He would come occasionally wearing this white belt, and they had typical jackets at the time, the members of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was clear from his story that his unit was quartered in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. He told me explicitly that he was in the hotel when the alarm was sounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The woman you mentioned, whose name we are not allowed to divulge, who was taken out of the house, you watched all this, were there any signs that she was trying to resist being expelled? Could you notice anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. Well, no characteristic signs, if I can use that term. Perhaps there were some, but it wasn't very noticeable, and I wasn't able to notice them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You then spoke about how the soldiers stormed your flat and threatened you with a pistol and told you to get into the bathroom. You said you didn't recognise them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform with HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But he didn't have any other insignia, did he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I didn't notice any other ones, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether he was a local man or somebody from elsewhere? Were you able to assess that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Could you tell me what you mean by local?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When I say local, I mean people from Vitez or the villages surrounding Vitez and -- or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, in that case he was a local.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You think he was a local?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: One hundred percent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you give us a description of his physique?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, he was a strongly built man, light skin, light hair, fair hair. He was rosy, had a rosy complexion. Maybe at that time he was under the effects of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about his age?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, he was about 25 to 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From your communication with the others, you couldn't hear the name or the nickname that was used?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, the other men didn't enter my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But they didn't shout to each other across the hallway?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. Just the man in front of the door at one point told him to hurry up, and said, "Hurry up, hurry up."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And although Kraljevic's name was written up on your front door, as Slaven Kraljevic told you to do, these men did not respect that, did they?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, when I say that the local people, regardless of the unit they belonged to, knew exactly who the Vitezovi were?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you think that some of the locals, despite the fact that you had put the name of Slaven Kraljevic out on your front door, that they would have gone against this -- that they knew him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, sir, nobody can guarantee that Slaven had not actually sent them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, although you thought that Slaven wanted to help you, you don't believe in his help?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I have no proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As we mentioned Darko Kraljevic and his unit, could we say that they were the masters of the situation in the part of town called Kolonija, which is somewhere behind your particular area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, that's a relative thing. To give my opinion, I haven't got any documents to back them up. So all I can say -- all I can do is repeat my own opinion, and that is that the HVO organisation itself was a very good one, and I think that the people sitting in the hotel were the masters of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But we do agree that the Vitezovi were a recognisable force in town?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way. If it was a force, well, I suppose they were a force then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were people afraid of them, SDK, the trench-digging? What did people say about them? Were they afraid? Was there a general sense of fear of them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I didn't notice anything that would be terrible. They did not stand out compared to the Jokers or some of the others. I didn't notice anything special about them in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have two more things to ask you. The first is the following: The apartment from which you were evicted by force, and you say that a soldier is still living there, and that you have undertaken legal steps to get your apartment back. Your father had the right to live there as a tenant's right, a legal tenant's right for the utilisation of that flat with his family?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, since 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't owned property, actually property owned by your father, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in keeping with the provisions, the steps you have taken, in the BiH Federation you have the right to get back your tenant's right to live there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing, please, witness, to avoid any misunderstandings. You were taken by the 3 Military Police from your apartment to the SDK building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From the SDK building to Zaselje, you were also taken by the Military Police. To Vranjska. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From Vranjska to Kratine, once again you were conveyed by the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the Military Police took you back to the SDK building, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, in view of the fact that it was very late at night, it was 12 or 1 a.m., it was complete darkness, I didn't see them taking us back. That is to say, I didn't see their insignia. I saw nothing on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what about the SDK, they -- it was members of the Military Police that stood guard over that building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it may be that you could help with a matter, while we are dealing with it. I wonder if we could have out the Exhibit D52/2. It's a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's obviously with the Registrar. I don't have my copy here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I have a similar map, Your Honour. If you could give me 20 seconds, I have it here. I have quite the same. Shall we use a brand new one without those markings or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've got it. Tell the usher there is no need to look for it any more. If you could put it on the ELMO, please. What I would be grateful for assistance with, and it may be that the witness can deal with this, is Krizancevo Selo, it was referred to in his evidence, it's been referred to before. There was an action there, we heard at one stage of the proceedings. I can't see anything of that sort marked, although there is a Sivrino Selo. What I want to know is where Krizancevo Selo is? Is it the same as Sivrino Selo, or is it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may assist, Your Honour, and we certainly could be assisted by this witness, I will tell you that it is not surprising that you can't find it, since it is not marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Krizancevo Selo is a part of a village which is called in a broader sense Sivrino Selo, but part Dubravica. And I will ask the witness to show us on the map, and I can do that as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness do it, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Usher, will you please move so to the centre, that Vitez is in the middle of the picture. Open the map. Open the map. All right. And now we need closer. Okay. That will do. Fine. Enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you, Mr. Ahmic, indicate to the Trial Chamber -- first find it on the map and then point it out to the Trial Chamber. Point out Krizancevo Selo. Which part of the village is referred to as Krizancevo Selo? And if I can help you, find Dubravica. Can you find Dubravica? It's lower to the left of Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is by the "B." The area called Krizancevo Selo is by the "B" of Dubravica. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, it's around about here. That's where it is. I think some houses -- no, that isn't a house. That's a peak, but around here [indicates]. That is where Krizancevo Selo is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are thinking of the peak?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, not the peak. A little under, below the peak, around this area here, these houses that are drawn in here. Are they houses? I think they are. So not down here by the peak, but down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the road. Go down by the road. Where is the school?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The school is somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it means that it is in the lower part?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I think it's around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's where it is. So below the junction?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I am able to point out with this pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As we are already there, shall we show the Trial Chamber, because this is also mentioned, where the railway station is?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The railway station is down here. It's the old railway station, but we keep referring to it as the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what about Novaci?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Novaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, because that name isn't on the map.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Novaci should be somewhere in this region here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's not relevant for this witness, but maybe we can also use opportunity -- the villages right from Sivrino Selo, which you can find on the map, Pirici and Vidovici. Later, perhaps, they will be relevant. They are mixed up. The names are switched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You say that the map is in error?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that is going to be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's well-known. I mean, even NATO knew that. We could check with the witness, if he knows, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, take a look at the villages of Pirici and Vidovici, to the right of Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the names of the villages correspond, or have they been reversed? Do you know that area? You know it better than I do, I suppose. If you can tell us, do so. If not, we'll ask someone else.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, my opinion is that you are, perhaps, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that you allow that a reversal has taken place?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: There is that possibility, yes, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Anything else, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. We'll adjourn now till just after half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We have no questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you were asked about, at the time of your mobilisation into the TO -- and I believe the time frame was roughly June of '92 -- if there were any Croats in the TO. Do you know whether or not, inasmuch as the HVO had been officially formed in April of '92, there were any Muslims from your area in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I also know that, but not a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So there, in fact, was a second existing military force principally opened to the Croats at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, that concludes your evidence. You are released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me deal with one or two administrative matters. Tomorrow we will sit, unless there's any submissions to the contrary, at 9, to finish at 12.30. As for the tapes which we were discussing yesterday, inquiries have shown that the translators can do the work of comparison, if they had the work now, by the 14th of February. But it does occur to me that if it's possible for the parties to agree on the matter, it wouldn't be necessary to trouble the translators with it. What is the feeling about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The issue is not, of course, whether the translation of the other tape would match the translation of the tape first produced but whether the sounds on the tapes are similar or identical. That is probably something that can be agreed by the Defence when they've listened to it, if that's the position. In each case, we would obviously like to listen to the tapes ourselves, preferably with a language speaker, I imagine, and that may resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, can that be done in the next few days? I say that because if we are going to have to ask Translation to listen to it, then the sooner we do it, the better. But it does occur to me that it should be possible of resolution without troubling them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The tape was to be given to us this morning. We don't have it as of yet. I would expect it would take -- over the weekend, we could get it done, report to the other side Monday. If there's an agreement Monday or Tuesday, we need not trouble the Translation Unit. If there's no agreement, we'll let them know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think that would be sensible. Where is the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My understanding, if I may be helpful, is the registrar was working with the technical booth. We were to have it this morning. It's somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could that be handed over? Perhaps I could ask the Registry if it could be handed over during the luncheon adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar will make sure that the problem will be resolved in agreement with the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, my forecast is this witness will probably be concluded this afternoon. The map was one of the topics we were planning to deal with tomorrow. Mr. Lopez-Terres, who has been dealing with that, discussed the matter with Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Stein, I think, and there is an agreement between them that it is likely to be or quite likely to be useful for a little more time to pass so that they can reach an agreement, and I don't think there's any intention on anybody's part to try and call any of the evidence of the map tomorrow; i.e., putting it off until later on. That leaves tomorrow free because of our loss of Stutt earlier in the week and our inability to replace him by a substantive witness. I'm very anxious, of course, not to lose any time that can be properly used for purposes of our case, and I've raised with the Defence whether some of the village binders could be considered tomorrow. I note theoretically they are down for determination on the 14th of February, but if we can get through some of them tomorrow, so much the better. I think the probabilities are that there are going to be a few of those binders that will be capable of being discussed tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with that when we know how we get on with the witness, provided we know what binders you want to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Jeremy Fleming, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY WARBURTON FLEMING
utterances.text: Jeremy Fleming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Fleming, were you in the army for 10 years in the infantry, then a manager for British Petroleum for some years, finally owning your own business, working in Afghanistan on de-mining, and then, or at least maybe in the meantime, but in 1992 being an ECMM monitor, first in Croatia, and then in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY WARBURTON FLEMING
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's right, I think, that you made diary notes during your time as an ECMM monitor; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY WARBURTON FLEMING
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And they were provided to this institution some considerable time ago, probably for another team. They haven't been looked at, as it happens, by this team, but have you had an opportunity to review them this morning to refresh your memory with what they contain?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY WARBURTON FLEMING
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it happen that the same document has also been used by you in relation to entirely different type of work, I think election monitoring work?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY WARBURTON FLEMING
utterances.text: That is correct. I was an election supervisor for the OSCE, and the document was used jointly, as a daily note reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness has used a diary to refresh his recollection, then he's using it somewhat as an aid to his testimony today. I wonder if the Defence could request that a copy be made available for our review, less, of course, entries of a personal nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's the usual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the position about the diary? Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't seen it. Nobody in our team has. But -- and he's only looked at it this morning to refresh his memory. I don't think very much has been added to what was in the summary, save some confirmation of earlier recollection and some other details. I know that the witness has no concerns himself about entries being seen, subject, of course, to entries about the other matter, obviously, not being made available and blocked to anyone else. Can I suggest that we simply see how his evidence goes, and if and where he refers to particular pages, they can, of course, be made available to the Defence, because there is no objection by the witness to that happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't seen it, but I have tied it together with an elastic band, and perhaps he can have it before him as an aide-memoire, if he seeks to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you first work in Split gathering information about military brigade headquarters, front lines of the HV, their discipline, morale, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY WARBURTON FLEMING
utterances.text: I arrived in Zagreb as a monitor in February, 1992, and it was only in May, 1992, that I was sent to Split to carry out those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The activities I've described were what you were engaged upon?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY WARBURTON FLEMING
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, what was your judgement of the professionalism or otherwise of Croatian troops, their discipline and, so far as you could judge, their arms?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY WARBURTON FLEMING
utterances.text: During the summer of 1992, when I was stationed in Split, a marked change in my perception of the professionalism of the Croatian forces took place. It was during at a time when the Vance-Owen Plan was being implemented, and in the town of Sinj there was a storage point for weapons which had been handed in by the forces, by the Croatian forces in a storage depot, and it was my job to track those weapons. Travelling to and fro from Split to Sinj, we found marching troops from the depot at Sinj, where they were being -- where the recruits were being trained as soldiers. And during that summer, it became noticeable that those bodies of troops were marching smartly, from their previous slightly untidy gait, and their uniforms were pressed and clean, their weapons, their personal rifles, AK-47s, seemed relatively new.
